problem: Social navigation is evaluated either with costly, hard-to-reproduce human surveys or with numerical metrics that have no consensus and unclear alignment with human perception of comfort, legibility, or smoothness.
motivation: If some quantitative metrics reliably track human judgments, they could serve as preliminary human-aligned benchmarks when large-scale surveys are infeasible. The authors analyse the relationship between 11 common metrics and 4 survey-based human metrics on real-robot experiments.
key_idea: Jointly analyse quantitative social-navigation metrics and human survey scores using K-means/ARI clustering and non-parametric correlation tests to find a small metric subset (QM*) that aligns with human perception.
insight: Raw use of all 11 metrics aligns poorly with human clusters (ARI -0.04), but selected subsets reach ARI 0.31-0.54, so metric selection matters. Proxemics occupancy (intimate/personal), average minimum distance to people, average robot speed and time-to-goal correlate best. Social Work is noisy and uncorrelated, and smoothness is poorly captured by any current metric, so new metrics are needed.
method: Real-robot dataset: Jackal robot with VICON tracking in a lab, 8 social scenarios (Passing, Overtaking, Crossing 1-3, Curious person, Narrow turn, Mixed), 3 runs each with different controller settings, giving 24 experiments.
Quantitative metrics (QM): 11 metrics (TTG, PL, CHC, ARV, SW, SW_s, AMD, proxemics occupancy for intimate/personal/social/public), rescaled to 0-1 per scenario relative to the best run.
Human metrics (HM): Unobtrusiveness, Friendliness, Smoothness, Avoidance foresight, rated on 5-point Likert scales by 70 participants watching 2D top-down GIFs, scaled to [0,1].

Clustering analysis: K-means on the QM and HM spaces separately (K in [2,5], silhouette score to choose K), Adjusted Rand Index between the two clusterings over all 2047 QM subsets, plus a cumulative ARI per metric.
Statistical analysis: Spearman, Kendall and Kruskal-Wallis tests between single QM and HM; Friedman and Wilcoxon tests validate that HM distinguishes runs.

setting.backbone: none (statistical analysis; K-means clustering; Jackal robot running various local planners)
setting.observation: VICON-tracked robot and human trajectories; survey participants view 2D top-down animations
setting.action_space: continuous velocity (v in [0,0.6] m/s, omega in [-1.5,1.5] rad/s)
setting.privileged: VICON ground-truth trajectories of robot and humans

numbers_note: No navigation benchmark results; only ARI/correlation analysis (e.g. best QM set ARI 0.54 vs 0.04 initial with all 11 metrics, K=2), which does not fit the benchmark schema.
results: Using all 11 metrics gives ARI -0.04 against human-based clusters, whereas the best subset (ARV, SW_s, PR_I, PR_PE, AMD) reaches ARI 0.54 at K=2. Intimate/personal proxemics, minimum distance to people, average speed and time-to-goal are consistently the most relevant. Smoothness is weakly captured and Social Work is noisy.
limitations: Only 24 trajectories in a small lab with 2D top-down video surveys, which lack the psychological effect of sharing physical space with the robot.
Human ratings are less consistent in complex scenarios like Narrow turn and Mixed; the subset selection is done on the same small data and may overfit.
